title: Сашу выгнали из квартиры  (Sasha Gets Evicted from Her Apartment)

segments.t: At the bar counter, Sasha confesses to Max that her landlady kicked her out of the apartment and demanded a huge sum for the water damage that she cannot afford. Before Max can figure out how to help her, Nastya grabs Kostya by the hand and drags him away.
Let's walk back through the scene line by line.
'Hey, how are things going?' Kostya quietly sends this casual greeting at the start of the beat using "privet" ("hi") — the everyday informal hello used between friends and close coworkers.
'Not bad.' Nastya politely drops this direct affirmation without hesitation using "da" ("yes") — a crisp "da" ("yes") that confirms the point without extra words.
'My landlady kicked me out of the apartment.' Kostya chimes in openly with a shrug, leaving no doubt about where he stands.
'What do you mean she kicked you out?' Nastya responds frankly beside Kostya and brings in "vygnala" ("kicked out", from "vygnat") as the key Russian word here.
'Wait, did you two really mop the floors?' Opening up smoothly at once, Kostya puts the question word "chto" right at the start so Nastya hears the focus immediately.
'And what are you going to do now?' Nastya questions straight out before Kostya can change the subject.
'I do not know, she said either...' Kostya weighs in wryly watching Nastya, grounding the moment in plain reality.
'I do not have that kind of money.' Nastya jumps in at once beside Kostya, letting the remark speak for itself.
'I really do not know.' Kostya jumps in promptly beside Nastya, grounding the moment in plain reality.

'It is fine, I will think of something.' Nastya directly sends this word of agreement while facing Kostya using "ladno" ("alright") — built from the old Russian root for harmony and order, used every day for "okay, fine".
'Kostik, come with me.' Reacting naturally with Kostya, spoken Russian compresses the whole thought into just 4 words, skipping the extra helper words English needs.
'Nastya, wait a second, are you serious?' Kostya presses frankly how Nastya expects that to work in practice.
'Are you actually serious right now?' Kostya follows up naturally with Max and chooses "seryezno" ("seriously", from the root "seryozno") so Max hears the exact meaning.
That wraps up this scene as sasha tells Max at the bar that her landlady evicted her over the flood damage, while Nastya pulls Kostya aside with an unexpected request. See you next time!
